entries.b3ee6a41d0e2ed6fc4d4cbea236705729333850f: <div sID="gen2290" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Lev.6" sID="Lev.6"/> <div eID="gen2290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2291" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2292" type="x-p"/> The first seven verses of this chapter might fitly have been added to the foregoing chapter, being a continuation of the law of the trespass-offering, and the putting of other cases in which it was to be offered; and with this end the instructions God gave concerning the several kinds of sacrifices that should be offered: and then at <reference osisRef="Lev.6.8">v. 8</reference> (which in the original begins a new section of the law) he comes to appoint the several rites and ceremonies concerning these sacrifices which had not been mentioned before. I. The burnt-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.8-Lev.6.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. II. The meat-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.11-Lev.6.18">ver. 11-18</reference>), particularly that at the consecration of the priest, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23">ver. 19-23</reference>. III. The sin-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.24-Lev.6.30">ver. 24</reference>, &c.
entries.896a9aaff6f45174be5eb26bbae18106d3e23354: <div eID="gen2292" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2291" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Law of the Trespass-Offering. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2293" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> If a soul sin, and commit a trespass against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and lie unto his neighbour in that which was delivered him to keep, or in fellowship, or in a thing taken away by violence, or hath deceived his neighbour; <hi type="super">3</hi> Or have found that which was lost, and lieth concerning it, and sweareth falsely; in any of all these that a man doeth, sinning therein: <hi type="super">4</hi> Then it shall be, because he hath sinned, and is guilty, that he shall restore that which he took violently away, or the thing which he hath deceitfully gotten, or that which was delivered him to keep, or the lost thing which he found, <hi type="super">5</hi> Or all that about which he hath sworn falsely; he shall even restore it in the principal, and shall add the fifth part more thereto, <hi type="italic">and</hi> give it unto him to whom it appertaineth, in the day of his trespass offering. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he shall bring his trespass offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , a ram without blemish out of the flock, with thy estimation, for a trespass offering, unto the priest: 7 And the priest shall make an atonement for him before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and it shall be forgiven him for any thing of all that he hath done in trespassing therein. <div eID="gen2293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2294" type="x-p"/> This is the latter part of the law of the trespass-offering: the former part, which concerned trespasses about holy things, we had in the close of the foregoing chapter; this concerns trespasses in common things. Observe here, <div eID="gen2294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2295" type="x-p"/> I. The trespass supposed, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.2-Lev.6.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. Though all the instances relate to our neighbour, yet it is called a <hi type="italic">trespass against the Lord,</hi> because, though the injury be done immediately to our neighbour, yet an affront is thereby given to his Maker and our Master. He that speaks evil of his brother is said to speak evil of the law, and consequently of the Law-maker, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.11">Jam. iv. 11</reference>. Though the person injured be ever so mean and despicable, and every way our inferior, yet the injury reflects upon that God who has made the command of loving our neighbour second to that of loving himself. The trespasses specified are, 1. Denying a trust: <hi type="italic">If a man lie unto his neighbour in that which was delivered him to keep,</hi> or, which is worse, which was lent him for his use. If we claim that as our own which is only borrowed, left in our custody, or committed to our care, this is a trespass <hi type="italic">against the Lord,</hi> who, for the benefit of human society, will have property and truth maintained. 2. Defrauding a partner: <hi type="italic">If a man lie in fellowship,</hi> claiming a sole interest in that wherein he has but a joint-interest. 3. Disowning a manifest wrong: <hi type="italic">If a man</hi> has the front to <hi type="italic">lie in a thing taken away by violence,</hi> which ordinarily cannot be hid. 4. Deceiving in commerce, or, as some think, by false accusation; if a man have <hi type="italic">deceitfully oppressed</hi> his neighbour, as some read it, either withholding what is due or extorting what is not. 5. Detaining what is found, and denying it (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.3">v. 3</reference>); if a man have <hi type="italic">found that which was lost,</hi> he must not call it his own presently, but endeavour to find out the owner, to whom it must be returned; this is doing as we would be done by: but he that <hi type="italic">lies concerning it,</hi> that falsely says he knows nothing of it, especially if he back this lie with a false oath, <hi type="italic">trespasseth against the Lord,</hi> who to every thing that is said is a witness, but in an oath he is the party appealed to, and highly affronted when he is called to witness to a lie. <div eID="gen2295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2296" type="x-p"/> II. The trespass-offering appointed. 1. <hi type="italic">In the day of his trespass-offering</hi> he must make satisfaction to his brother. This must be first done <hi type="italic">if thy brother hath aught against thee: Because he hath sinned and is guilty,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.4-Lev.6.5">v. 4, 5</reference>), that is, is convicted of his guilt by his own conscience, and is touched with remorse for it; seeing himself guilty before God, let him faithfully restore all that he has got by fraud or oppression, with a fifth part added, to make amends to the owner for the loss and trouble he had sustained in the mean time; let him account both for debt and damages. Note, Where wrong has been done restitution must be made; and till it is made to the utmost of our power, or an equivalent accepted by the person wronged, we cannot have the comfort of the forgiveness of the sin; for the keeping of what is unjustly got avows the taking, and both together make but one continued act of unrighteousness. To repent is to undo what we have done amiss, which (whatever we pretend) we cannot be said to do till we restore what has been got by it, as Zaccheus (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.8">Luke xix. 8</reference>), and make satisfaction for the wrong done. 2. He must <hi type="italic">then come and offer his gift,</hi> must <hi type="italic">bring his trespass-offering to the Lord</hi> whom he had offended; and the priest must make an atonement for him, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.6-Lev.6.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. This trespass-offering could not, of itself, make satisfaction for sin, nor reconciliation between God and the sinner, but as it signified the atonement that was to be made by our Lord Jesus, when he should make his soul <hi type="italic">an offering or sin,</hi> a <hi type="italic">trespass-offering;</hi> it is the same word that is here used, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>. The trespasses here mentioned are trespasses still against the law of Christ, which insists as much upon justice and truth as ever the law of nature or the law of Moses did; and though now we may have them pardoned without a trespass-offering, yet not without true repentance, restitution, reformation, and a humble faith in the righteousness of Christ: and, if any make the more bold with these sins because they are not now put to the expense of a trespass-offering for them, they turn the grace of God into wantonness, and so bring upon themselves a swift destruction. The Lord is the avenger of all such, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.6">1 Thess. iv. 6</reference>.
entries.21dc7bd1ec55dbcf276f6f487f5961db3392a8de: <div eID="gen2296" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Law of the Burnt-Offering. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2297" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">9</hi> Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the burnt offering: It <hi type="italic">is</hi> the burnt offering, because of the burning upon the altar all night unto the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be burning in it. 10 And the priest shall put on his linen garment, and his linen breeches shall he put upon his flesh, and take up the ashes which the fire hath consumed with the burnt offering on the altar, and he shall put them beside the altar. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he shall put off his garments, and put on other garments, and carry forth the ashes without the camp unto a clean place. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the fire upon the altar shall be burning in it; it shall not be put out: and the priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and lay the burnt offering in order upon it; and he shall burn thereon the fat of the peace offerings. <hi type="super">13</hi> The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out. <div eID="gen2297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2298" type="x-p"/> Hitherto we have had the instructions which Moses was directed to give to the people concerning the sacrifices; but here begin the instructions he was to give to the priests; he must <hi type="italic">command Aaron and his sons,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.9">v. 9</reference>. The priests were rulers in the house of God, but these rulers must be ruled; and those that had the command of others must themselves be commanded. Let ministers remember that not only commissions, but commands, were given to Aaron and his sons, who must be in subjection to them. <div eID="gen2298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2299" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have the law of the burnt-offering, as far as it was the peculiar care of the priests. The daily sacrifice of a lamb, which was offered morning and evening for the whole congregation, is here chiefly referred to. <div eID="gen2299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2300" type="x-p"/> I. The priest must take care of the ashes of the burnt-offering, that they be decently disposed of, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.10-Lev.6.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. He must clear the altar of them every morning, and put them on the east side of the altar, which was furthest from the sanctuary; this he must do in his linen garment, which he always wore when he did any service at the altar; and then he must shift himself, and put on other garments, either such as were his common wear, or (as some think) other priestly garments less honourable, and must <hi type="italic">carry the ashes into a clean place without the camp.</hi> Now, 1. God would have this done, for the honour of his altar and the sacrifices that were burnt upon it. Even the ashes of the sacrifices must be preserved, to testify the regard God had to it; by the burnt-offering <hi type="italic">he</hi> was honoured, and therefore thus <hi type="italic">it</hi> was honoured. And some think that this care which was taken of the ashes of the sacrifice typified the burial of our Saviour; his dead body (the ashes of his sacrifice) was carefully laid up in a garden, in a new sepulchre, which was a <hi type="italic">clean place.</hi> It was also requisite that the altar should be kept as clean as might be; the fire upon it would burn the better, and it is decent in a house to have a clean fire-side. 2. God would have the priests themselves to keep it so, to teach them and us to stoop to the meanest services for the honour of God and of his altar. The priest himself must not only kindle the fire, but clean the hearth, and carry out the ashes. God's servants must think nothing below them but sin. <div eID="gen2300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2301" type="x-p"/> II. The priest must take care of the fire upon the altar, that it be kept <hi type="italic">always burning.</hi> This is much insisted on here (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.9">v. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.12">12</reference>), and this express law is given: <hi type="italic">The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar, it shall never go out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.13">v. 13</reference>. We may suppose that no day passed without some extraordinary sacrifices, which were always offered between the morning and evening lamb; so that from morning to night the fire on the altar was kept up of course. But to preserve it <hi type="italic">all night unto the morning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.9">v. 9</reference>) required some care. Those that keep good houses never let their kitchen fire go out; therefore God would thus give an instance of his good house-keeping. The first fire upon the altar came <hi type="italic">from heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.24">ch. ix. 24</reference>), so that by keeping that up continually with a constant supply of fuel all their sacrifices throughout all their generations might be said to be consumed with that fire from heaven, in token of God's acceptance. If, through carelessness, they should ever let it go out, they could not expect to have it so kindled again. Accordingly the Jews tell us that the fire never did go out upon the altar, till the captivity in Babylon. This is referred to <reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">Isa. xxxi. 9</reference>, where God is said <hi type="italic">to have his fire in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem.</hi> By this law we are taught to keep up in our minds a constant disposition to all acts of piety and devotion, an habitual affection to divine things, so as to be always ready to every good word and work. We must not only not <hi type="italic">quench the Spirit,</hi> but we must <hi type="italic">stir up the gift</hi> that is in us. Though we be not always sacrificing, yet we must keep the fire of holy love always burning; and thus we must pray always.
entries.acca1c5a9ad9daa016bbc80b63faa72d58cd121a: <div eID="gen2301" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Law of the Meat-Offering. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2302" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the meat offering: the sons of Aaron shall offer it before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , before the altar. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he shall take of it his handful, of the flour of the meat offering, and of the oil thereof, and all the frankincense which <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the meat offering, and shall burn <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the altar <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sweet savour, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the memorial of it, unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">16</hi> And the remainder thereof shall Aaron and his sons eat: with unleavened bread shall it be eaten in the holy place; in the court of the tabernacle of the congregation they shall eat it. <hi type="super">17</hi> It shall not be baken with leaven. I have given it <hi type="italic">unto them for</hi> their portion of my offerings made by fire; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> most holy, as <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sin offering, and as the trespass offering. <hi type="super">18</hi> All the males among the children of Aaron shall eat of it. <hi type="italic">It shall be</hi> a statute for ever in your generations concerning the offerings of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made by fire: every one that toucheth them shall be holy. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">20</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the offering of Aaron and of his sons, which they shall offer unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the day when he is anointed; the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour for a meat offering perpetual, half of it in the morning, and half thereof at night. <hi type="super">21</hi> In a pan it shall be made with oil; <hi type="italic">and when it is</hi> baken, thou shalt bring it in: <hi type="italic">and</hi> the baken pieces of the meat offering shalt thou offer <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">22</hi> And the priest of his sons that is anointed in his stead shall offer it: <hi type="italic">it is</hi> a statute for ever unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; it shall be wholly burnt. <hi type="super">23</hi> For every meat offering for the priest shall be wholly burnt: it shall not be eaten. <div eID="gen2302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2303" type="x-p"/> The meat-offering was either that which was offered by the people or that by the priests at their consecration. Now, <div eID="gen2303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2304" type="x-p"/> I. As to the common meat-offering, <div eID="gen2304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2305" type="x-p"/> 1. Only a handful of it was to be burnt upon the altar; all the rest was allowed to the priests for their food. The law of the burnt-offerings was such as imposed upon the priests a great deal of care and work, but allowed them little profit; for the flesh was wholly burnt, and the priests had nothing but the skin. But to make them amends the greatest part of the meat-offering was their own. The burning of a handful of it upon the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.15">v. 15</reference>) was ordered before, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.2">ch. ii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.9">9</reference>. Here the remainder of it is consigned to the priests, the servants of God's house: <hi type="italic">I have given it unto them for their portion of my offerings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.17">v. 17</reference>. Note, (1.) It is the will of God that his ministers should be well provided for with food convenient; and what is given to them he accepts as offered to himself, if it be done with a single eye. (2.) All Christians, being spiritual priests, do themselves share in the spiritual sacrifices they offer. It is not God that is the gainer by them; the handful burnt upon the altar was not worth speaking of, in comparison with the priests' share; we ourselves are the gainers by our religious services. Let God have all the frankincense, and the priests shall have the flour and the oil; what we give to God the praise and glory of we may take to ourselves the comfort and benefit of. <div eID="gen2305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2306" type="x-p"/> 2. The laws concerning the eating of it were, (1.) That it must be <hi type="italic">eaten unleavened,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.16">v. 16</reference>. What was offered to God must have no leaven in it, and the priests must have it as the altar had it, and no otherwise. Thus must we keep the feasts of the Lord with the <hi type="italic">unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.</hi> (2.) It must be eaten in <hi type="italic">the court of the tabernacle</hi> (here called the <hi type="italic">holy place</hi>), in some room prepared by the side of the court for this purpose. It was a great crime to carry any of it out of the court. The very eating of it was a sacred rite, by which they were to honour God, and therefore it must be done in a religious manner, and with a holy reverence, which was preserved by confining it to the holy place. (3.) The males only must eat of it, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.18">v. 18</reference>. Of the less holy things, as the first-fruits and tithes, and the shoulder and breasts of the peace-offerings, the <hi type="italic">daughters</hi> of the priests might eat, for they might be carried out of the court; but this was of the most holy things, which being to be eaten only in the tabernacle, the <hi type="italic">sons</hi> of Aaron only might eat of it. (4.) The priests only that were clean might eat of it: <hi type="italic">Every one that toucheth them shall be holy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.18">v. 18</reference>. Holy things for holy persons. Some read it, <hi type="italic">Every thing that toucheth it shall be holy:</hi> Al the furniture of the table on which these holy things were eaten must be appropriated to that use only, and never after used as common things. <div eID="gen2306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2307" type="x-p"/> II. As to the consecration meat-offering, which was offered for the priests themselves, it was to be <hi type="italic">wholly burnt, and none of it eaten,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.23">v. 23</reference>. It comes in here as an exception to the foregoing law. It should seem that this law concerning the meat-offering of initiation did not only oblige the high priest to offer it, and on that day only that he was anointed, and so for his successors in the day they were anointed; but the Jewish writers say that by this law every priest, on the day he first entered upon his ministry, was bound to offer this meat-offering,—that the high priest was bound to offer it every day of his life, from the day in which he was anointed,—and that it was to be offered besides the meat-offering that attended the morning and evening sacrifice, because it is said here to be a <hi type="italic">meat-offering perpetual,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.20">v. 20</reference>. Josephus says, "The high priest sacrificed twice every day at his own charges, and this was his sacrifice." Note, Those whom God has advanced above others in dignity and power ought to consider that he expects more from them than from others, and should attend to every intimation of service to be done for him. The meat-offering of the priest was to be baked as if it were to be eaten, and yet it must be wholly burnt. Though the priest that ministered was to be paid for serving the people, yet there was no reason that he should be paid for serving the high priest, who was the father of the family of the priests, and whom therefore any priest should take a pleasure in serving gratis. Nor was it fit that the priests should eat of the offerings of a priest; for as the sins of the people were typically transferred to the priests, which was signified by their eating of their offerings (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.8">Hos. iv. 8</reference>), so the sins of the priests must be typically transferred to the altar, which therefore must eat up all their offerings. We are all undone, both ministers and people, if we must <hi type="italic">bear our own iniquity;</hi> nor could we have had any comfort or hope if God had not laid on his dear Son the iniquity of us all, and he is both the priest and the altar.
entries.e4d137177ae2d58492511f657ee446e5acbe5ebf: <div eID="gen2307" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Law of the Sin-Offering. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2308" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, 25 Speak unto Aaron and to his sons, saying, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the sin offering: In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it <hi type="italic">is</hi> most holy. 26 The priest that offereth it for sin shall eat it: in the holy place shall it be eaten, in the court of the tabernacle of the congregation. 27 Whatsoever shall touch the flesh thereof shall be holy: and when there is sprinkled of the blood thereof upon any garment, thou shalt wash that whereon it was sprinkled in the holy place. 28 But the earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken: and if it be sodden in a brazen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water. 29 All the males among the priests shall eat thereof: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> most holy. 30 And no sin offering, whereof <hi type="italic">any</hi> of the blood is brought into the tabernacle of the congregation to reconcile <hi type="italic">withal</hi> in the holy <hi type="italic">place,</hi> shall be eaten: it shall be burnt in the fire. <div eID="gen2308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2309" type="x-p"/> We have here so much of the law of the sin-offering as did peculiarly concern the priests that offered it. As, 1. That it must be killed <hi type="italic">in the place where the burnt-offering was killed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.25">v. 25</reference>), that is, on the north side of the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.11">ch. i. 11</reference>), which, some think typified the crucifying of Christ on mount Calvary, which was on the north side of Jerusalem. 2. That the priest who offered it for the sinner was (with his sons, or other priests, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.29">v. 29</reference>) to eat the flesh of it, after the blood and fat had been offered to God, in the <hi type="italic">court of the tabernacle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.26">v. 26</reference>. Hereby they were to <hi type="italic">bear the iniquity of the congregation,</hi> as it is explained, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.17">ch. x. 17</reference>. 3. The blood of the sin-offering was with great reverence to be washed out of the clothes on which it happened to light (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.27">v. 27</reference>), which signified the awful regard we ought to have to the blood of Christ, not counting it a common thing; that blood must be sprinkled on the conscience, not on the raiment. 4. The vessel in which the flesh of the sin-offering was boiled must be broken if it were an earthen one, and, if a brazen one, well washed, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.28">v. 28</reference>. This intimated that the defilement was not wholly taken away by the offering, but did rather cleave to it, such was the weakness and deficiency of those sacrifices; but the blood of Christ thoroughly cleanses from all sin, and after it there needs no cleansing. 5. That all this must be understood of the common sin-offerings, not of those for the priest, or the body of the congregation, either occasional, or stated upon the day of atonement; for it had been before ordained, and was now ratified, that if the blood of the offering was brought into the holy place, as it was in those extraordinary cases, the flesh was not to be eaten, but burnt without the camp, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.30">v. 30</reference>. Hence the apostle infers the advantage we have under the gospel above what they had under the law; for though the blood of Christ was <hi type="italic">brought into the tabernacle, to reconcile within the holy place,</hi> yet we have a right by faith to <hi type="italic">eat of the altar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.10-Heb.13.12">Heb. xiii. 10-12</reference>), and so to take the comfort of the great propitiation.  <chapter eID="Lev.6"/> <div eID="gen2309" type="x-p"/>

entries.7feb735542e0e3b2150e75bd7a33442418bc9bbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1021"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.6.1-Lev.6.7">Le 6:1-7</reference>. Trespass Offering for Sins Done Wittingly.</title> <div sID="gen1411" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1021"/><hi type="bold">2-7. If a soul sin, and commit a trespass against the Lord--</hi>This law, the record of which should have been joined with the previous chapter, was given concerning things stolen, fraudulently gotten, or wrongfully kept. The offender was enjoined to make restitution of the articles to the rightful owner, along with a fifth part out of his own possessions. But it was not enough thus to repair the injury done to a neighbor and to society; he was required to bring a trespass offering, as a token of sorrow and penitence for having hurt the cause of religion and of God. That trespass offering was a ram without blemish, which was to be made on the altar of burnt offerings, and the flesh belonged to the priests. This penalty was equivalent to a mitigated fine; but being associated with a sacred duty, the form in which the fine was inflicted served the important purpose of rousing attention to the claims and reviving a sense of responsibility to God. <div eID="gen1411" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c0b7c2dc4fcd60c0360c4e435dbe0388f87b5b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1022"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.6.8-Lev.6.13">Le 6:8-13</reference>. The Law of the Burnt Offering.</title> <div sID="gen1412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1022"/><hi type="bold">9. Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This ... law of the burnt offering--</hi>In this passage Moses received instructions to be delivered to the priests respecting their official duties, and first the burnt offering--Hebrew, "a sacrifice, which went up in smoke." The daily service consisted of two lambs, one offered in the morning at sunrise, the other in the evening, when the day began to decline. Both of them were consumed on the altar by means of a slow fire, before which the pieces of the sacrifice were so placed that they fed it all night. At all events, the observance of this daily sacrifice on the altar of burnt offering was a daily expression of national repentance and faith. The fire that consumed these sacrifices had been kindled from heaven at the consecration of the tabernacle [Le 9:24], and to keep it from being extinguished and the sacrifices from being burned with common fire, strict injunctions are here given respecting not only the removal of the ashes [Le 6:10, 11], but the approaching near to the fireplace in garments that were not officially "holy." <div eID="gen1412" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9370a667c44d690e9aae844a23e29cf8d272fa1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1023"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.6.14-Lev.6.18">Le 6:14-18</reference>. The Law of the Meat Offering.</title> <div sID="gen1413" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1023"/><hi type="bold">14-18. this is the law of the meat offering--</hi>Though this was a provision for the priests and their families, it was to be regarded as "most holy"; and the way in which it was prepared was: on any meat offerings being presented, the priest carried them to the altar, and taking a handful from each of them as an oblation, he salted and burnt it on the altar; the residue became the property of the priests, and was the food of those whose duty it was to attend on the service. They themselves as well as the vessels from which they ate were typically holy, and they were not at liberty to partake of the meat offering while they labored under any ceremonial defilement. <div eID="gen1413" type="x-p"/>
entries.95fb1a64a245425ce48b4c3b29cc1c40776babf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1024"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23">Le 6:19-23</reference>. The High Priest's Meat Offering.</title> <div sID="gen1414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1024"/><hi type="bold">20. This is the offering of Aaron, and of his sons--</hi>the daily meat offering of the high priest; for though his sons are mentioned along with him, it was probably only those of his descendants who succeeded him in that high office that are meant. It was to be offered, one half of it in the morning and the other half in the evening--being daily laid by the ministering priest on the altar of burnt offering, where, being dedicated to God, it was wholly consumed. This was designed to keep him and the other attendant priests in constant remembrance, that though they were typically expiating the sins of the people, their own persons and services could meet with acceptance only through faith, which required to be daily nourished and strengthened from above. <div eID="gen1414" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7f4a9b829e2fd12a3b953eb549e3fab844c1d62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1025"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.6.21-Lev.6.30">Le 6:21-30</reference>. The Law of the Sin Offering.</title> <div sID="gen1415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1025"/><hi type="bold">25-28. This is the law of the sin offering--</hi>It was slain, and the fat and inwards, after being washed and salted, were burnt upon the altar. But the rest of the carcass belonged to the officiating priest. He and his family might feast upon it--only, however, within the precincts of the tabernacle; and none else were allowed to partake of it but the members of a priestly family--and not even they, if under any ceremonial defilement. The flesh on all occasions was boiled or sodden, with the exception of the paschal lamb, which was roasted [Ex 12:8, 9]; and if an earthen vessel had been used, it being porous and likely to imbibe some of the liquid particles, it was to be broken; if a metallic pan had been used it was to be scoured and washed with the greatest care, not because the vessels had been defiled, but the reverse--because the flesh of the sin offering having been boiled in them, those vessels were now too sacred for ordinary use. The design of all these minute ceremonies was to impress the minds, both of priests and people, with a sense of the evil nature of sin and the care they should take to prevent the least taint of its impurities clinging to them. <chapter eID="Lev.6"/>

entries.899f3934354ae97315f26b8bb3b54ce7077080eb: <div eID="gen4369" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4370" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4371" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4371" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4370" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4372" type="x-p"/> Laws relative to detention of property entrusted to the care of another, to robbery, and deceit, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.1">Lev 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.2">Lev 6:2</reference>; finding of goods lost, keeping them from their owner, and swearing falsely, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.3">Lev 6:3</reference>. Such a person shall not only restore what he has thus unlawfully gotten, but shall add a fifth part of the value of the property besides, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.4">Lev 6:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.5">Lev 6:5</reference>; and bring a ram without blemish, for a trespass-offering to the Lord, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.6">Lev 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.7">Lev 6:7</reference>. Laws relative to the burnt-offering and the perpetual fire, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.8-Lev.6.13">Lev 6:8-13</reference>. Law of the meat-offering, and who may lawfully eat of it, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.14-Lev.6.18">Lev 6:14-18</reference>. Laws relative to the offerings of Aaron and his sons and their successors, on the day of their anointing, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23">Lev 6:19-23</reference>. Laws relative to the sin-offering, and those who might eat of it, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.24-Lev.6.30">Lev 6:24-30</reference>.
entries.5bc796c2ea93899593a15b5968651f80ee7736a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen4372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4373" type="x-p"/> Lie unto his neighbor, etc. - This must refer to a case in which a person delivered his property to his neighbor to be preserved for him, and took no witness to attest the delivery of the goods; such a person therefore might deny that he had ever received such goods, for he who had deposited them with him could bring no proof of the delivery. On the other hand, a man might accuse his neighbor of detaining property which had never been confided to him, or, after having been confided, had been restored again; hence the law here is very cautious on these points: and because in many cases it was impossible to come at the whole truth without a direct revelation from God, which should in no common case be expected, the penalties are very moderate; for in such cases, even when guilt was discovered, the man might not be so criminal as appearances might intimate. See the law concerning this laid down and explained on <reference osisRef="Exo.22.7">Exo 22:7</reference> (note), etc.
entries.24482e112a5e7a8307b92c42b384a7a6640f037e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen4373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4374" type="x-p"/> Have found that which was lost - The Roman lawyers laid it down as a sound maxim of jurisprudence, "that he who found any property and applied it to his own use, should be considered as a thief whether he knew the owner or not; for in their view the crime was not lessened, supposing the finder was totally ignorant of the right owner." Qui alienum quid jacens lucri faciendi causa sustulit, furti obstringitur, sive scit, cujus sit, sive ignoravit; nihil enim ad furtum minuendum, facit, quod, cujus sit, ignoret - Digestor, lib. xlvii., Tit. ii., de furtis, Leg. xliii., sec. 4. On this subject every honest man must say, that the man who finds any lost property, and does not make all due inquiry to find out the owner, should, in sound policy, be treated as a thief. It is said of the Dyrbaeans, a people who inhabited the tract between Bactria and India, that if they met with any lost property, even on the public road, they never even touched it. This was actually the case in this kingdom in the time of Alfred the Great, about a. d. 888; so that golden bracelets hung up on the public roads were untouched by the finger of rapine. One of Solon's laws was, Take not up what you laid not down. How easy to act by this principle in case of finding lost property: "This is not mine, and it would be criminal to convert it to my use unless the owner be dead and his family extinct." When all due inquiry is made, if no owner can be found, the lost property may be legally considered to be the property of the finder.
entries.9fa453a7f968ef41238f35673bd583a95055f163: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen4374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4375" type="x-p"/> All that about which he hath sworn falsely - This supposes the case of a man who, being convicted by his own conscience, comes forward and confesses his sin. <div eID="gen4375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4376" type="x-p"/> Restore it in the principal - The property itself if still remaining, or the full value of it, to which a fifth part more was to be added.
entries.72a5573805e51e2074276092814d8a3ac9b56a2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen4376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4377" type="x-p"/> With thy estimation - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.5.15">Lev 5:15</reference>.
entries.58aaf79738bcbdcc7bc03c2a4040d5d61c68ba83: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen4377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4378" type="x-p"/> And the Lord spake unto Moses - At this verse the Jews begin the 25th section of the law; and here, undoubtedly, the 6th chapter should commence, as the writer enters upon a new subject, and the preceding verses belong to the fifth chapter. The best edited Hebrew Bibles begin the 6th chapter at this verse.
entries.974881e022ef8c472deeb940482b069020372e5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen4378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4379" type="x-p"/> This is the law of the burnt-offering - This law properly refers to that burnt-offering which was daily made in what was termed the morning and evening sacrifice; and as he had explained the nature of this burnt-offering in general, with its necessary ceremonies, as far as the persons who brought them were concerned, he now takes up the same in relation to the priests who were to receive them from the hands of the offerer, and present them to the Lord on the altar of burnt-offerings. <div eID="gen4379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4380" type="x-p"/> Because of the burning upon the altar all night - If the burnt-offering were put all upon the fire at once, it could not be burning all night. We may therefore reasonably conclude that the priests sat up by turns the whole night, and fed the fire with portions of this offering till the whole was consumed, which they would take care to lengthen out till the time of the morning sacrifice. The same we may suppose was done with the morning sacrifice; it was also consumed by piecemeal through the whole day, till the time of offering the evening sacrifice. Thus there was a continual offering by fire unto the Lord; and hence in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.13">Lev 6:13</reference> it is said: The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar, it shall never go out. If at any time any extraordinary offerings were to be made, the daily sacrifice was consumed more speedily, in order to make room for such extra offerings. See more on this subject in Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.6.23">Lev 6:23</reference> (note). The Hebrew doctors teach that no sacrifice was ever offered in the morning before the morning sacrifice; and none, the passover excepted, ever offered in the evening after the evening sacrifice; for all sacrifices were made by day-light. The fat seems to have been chiefly burned in the night season, for the greater light and convenience of keeping the fire alive, which could not be so easily done in the night as in the day time.
entries.2a8b0b0ece222c3c1270bbf5e18aae5447ffb993: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen4380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4381" type="x-p"/> And put on other garments - The priests approached the altar in their holiest garments; when carrying the ashes, etc., from the altar, they put on other garments, the holy garments being only used in the holy place. <div eID="gen4381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4382" type="x-p"/> Clean place - A place where no dead carcasses, dung, or filth of any kind was laid; for the ashes were holy, as being the remains of the offerings made by fire unto the Lord.
entries.c56b7ab83323225a64cfb763e9c55171af3fc420: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen4382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4383" type="x-p"/> The fire shall ever be burning - See on <reference osisRef="Lev.6.9">Lev 6:9</reference> (note) and <reference osisRef="Lev.6.20">Lev 6:20</reference> (note). In imitation of this perpetual fire, the ancient Persian Magi, and their descendants the Parses, kept up a perpetual fire; the latter continue it to the present day. This is strictly enjoined in the Zend Avesta, which is a code of laws as sacred among them as the Pentateuch is among the Jews. A Sagnika Brahmin preserves the fire that was kindled at his investiture with the poita, and never suffers it to go out, using the same fire at his wedding and in all his burnt-offerings, till at length his body is burnt with it - Ward's Customs.
entries.bfdf19d3547133bbeffe216c492d9eaf32cb8340: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen4383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4384" type="x-p"/> The meat-offering - See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Lev 2:1</reference> (note), etc.
entries.794bf6919db3b60cd83c20940f4332446304c007: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen4384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4385" type="x-p"/> His handful of the flour - An omer of flour, which was the tenth part of an ephah, and equal to about three quarts of our measure, was the least quantity that could be offered even by the poorest sort, and this was generally accompanied with a log of oil, which was a little more than half a pint. This quantity both of flour and oil might be increased at pleasure, but no less could be offered.
entries.34553e2a36febe6d6b0e41166963667fcabdf999: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen4385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4386" type="x-p"/> In the day when he is anointed - Not only in that day, but from that day forward, for this was to them and their successors a statute for ever. See <reference osisRef="Lev.6.22">Lev 6:22</reference>.
entries.69c051441fe9ed4f8e83e47f8055812ac35292be: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen4386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4387" type="x-p"/> For every meat-offering for the priest shall be wholly burnt - Whatever the priest offered was wholly the Lord's, and therefore must be entirely consumed: the sacrifices of the common people were offered to the Lord, but the priests partook of them; and thus they who ministered at the altar were fed by the altar. Had the priests been permitted to live on their own offerings as they did on those of the people, it would have been as if they had offered nothing, as they would have taken again to themselves what they appeared to give unto the Lord. Theodoret says that this marked "the high perfection which God required in the ministers of his sanctuary," as his not eating of his own sin-offering supposes him to stand free from all sin; but a better reason is given by Mr. Ainsworth: "The people's meat-offering was eaten by the priests that made atonement for them, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.15">Lev 6:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.16">Lev 6:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.7">Lev 7:7</reference>; but because no priest, being a sinner, could make atonement for himself, therefore his meat-offering might not be eaten, but all burnt on the altar, to teach him to expect salvation, not by his legal service or works, but by Christ; for the eating of the sin-offering figured the bearing of the sinner's iniquity;" <reference osisRef="Lev.10.17">Lev 10:17</reference>.
entries.241fe2a6a55e60346edd5b153cb4dbf05df36dd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen4387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4388" type="x-p"/> In the place where the burnt-offering is killed, etc. - The place here referred to was the north side of the altar. See <reference osisRef="Lev.1.11">Lev 1:11</reference>.
entries.97b0601f8a05d468cee95a02f350ded8844224c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen4388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4389" type="x-p"/> The priest - shall eat it - From the expostulation of Moses with Aaron, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.17">Lev 10:17</reference>, we learn that the priest, by eating the sin-offering of the people, was considered as bearing their sin, and typically removing it from them: and besides, this was a part of their maintenance, or what the Scripture calls their inheritance; see <reference osisRef="Eze.44.27-Eze.44.30">Eze 44:27-30</reference>. This was afterwards greatly abused; for improper persons endeavored to get into the priest's office merely that they might get a secular provision, which is a horrible profanity in the sight of God. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.36">1Sam 2:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.12">Jer 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.34.2-Eze.34.4">Eze 34:2-4</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Hos.4.8">Hos 4:8</reference>.
entries.8f7cc2b293e35a2b14e76b066ae2aeebfe06db76: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen4389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4390" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever shall touch the flesh thereof shall be holy - The following note of Mr. Ainsworth is not less judicious than it is pious: - "All this rite was peculiar to the sin-offering, (whether it were that which was to be eaten, or that which was to be burnt), above all the other most holy things. As the sin-offering in special sort figured Christ, who was made sin for us, (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Cor 5:21</reference>), so this ordinance for all that touched the flesh of the sin-offering to be holy, the garments sprinkled with the blood to be washed, the vessels wherein the flesh was boiled to be broken, or scoured and rinsed - taught a holy use of this mystery of our redemption, whereof they that are made partakers ought to be washed, cleansed, and sanctified by the Spirit of God; that we possess our vessels in holiness and honor, and yield not our members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin," <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.4">1Thes 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.13">Rom 6:13</reference>.
entries.dc71ff71170c18a8abbb6ce834d5134313569572: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen4390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4391" type="x-p"/> The earthen vessel - shall be broken - Calmet states that this should be considered as implying the vessels brought by individuals to the court of the temple or tabernacle, and not of the vessels that belonged to the priests for the ordinary service. That the people dressed their sacrifices sometimes in the court of the tabernacle, he gathers from <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.13">1Sam 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.14">1Sam 2:14</reference>, to which the reader is desired to refer. In addition to what has been already said on the different subjects in this chapter, it may be necessary to notice a few more particulars. The perpetual meat-offering, מנחה תמיד minchah tamid, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.20">Lev 6:20</reference>, the perpetual fire, אש תמיד esh tamid, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.13">Lev 6:13</reference>, and the perpetual burnt-offering, עלת תמיד olath tamid, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.42">Exo 29:42</reference>, translated by the Septuagint θυσια διαπαντος, πυο διαπαντος, and ὁλοκαυτωσις and ὁλοκαυτωμα διαπαντος, all cast much light on <reference osisRef="Heb.7.25">Heb 7:25</reference>, where it is said, Christ is able to save them to the uttermost (εις το παντελες, perpetually, to all intents and purposes) that come unto God by him; seeing he ever liveth (παντοτε ζων, he is perpetually living) to make intercession for them; in which words there is a manifest allusion to the perpetual minchah, the perpetual fire, and the perpetual burnt-offering, mentioned here by Moses. As the minchah, or gratitude-offering should be perpetual, so our gratitude for the innumerable mercies of God should be perpetual. As the burnt-offering must be perpetual, so should the sacrifice of our blessed Lord be considered as a perpetual offering, that all men, in all ages, should come unto God through him who is ever living, in his sacrificial character, to make intercession for men; and who is therefore represented even in the heavens as the Lamb just slain, standing before the throne, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Rev 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19-Heb.10.22">Heb 10:19-22</reference>. And as the fire on the altar must be perpetual, so should the influences of the Holy Spirit in every member of the Church, and the flame of pure devotion in the hearts of believers, be ever energetic and permanent. A continual sacrifice for continual successive generations of sinners was essentially necessary. Continual influences of the Holy Spirit on the souls of men were essentially necessary to apply and render effectual this atonement, to the salvation of the soul. And incessant gratitude for the ineffable love of God, manifested by his unspeakable gift, is surely required of all those who have tasted that the Lord is gracious. Reader, dost thou feel thy obligations to thy Maker? Does the perpetual fire burn on the altar of thy heart? Art thou ever looking unto Jesus, and beholding, by faith, the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world? And dost thou feel the influences of his Spirit, at all times witnessing with thy spirit that thou art his child, and exciting thee to acts of gratitude and obedience? If not, of what benefit has the religion of Christ been to thee to the present day? Of a contrary state to that referred to above, it may be well said, This is not the way to heaven, for the way of life is above to the wise, that they may depart from the snares of death beneath. Arise, therefore, and shake thyself from the dust; and earnestly call upon the Lord thy God, that he may save thy soul, and that thou fall not into the bitter pains of an eternal death.  <chapter eID="Lev.6"/> <div eID="gen4391" type="x-p"/>

entries.210dedc1bd5ad4f39ca2d51418a8c8108f6a1f9c: <div eID="gen1212" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">2. Special Instructions Concerning the Sacrifices for the Priests - Leviticus 6-7</title> <div sID="gen1213" type="x-p"/> The instructions contained in these two chapters were made known to “<hi type="italic">Aaron and his sons</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.9">Lev 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.20">Lev 6:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.25">Lev 6:25</reference>), i.e., to the priests, and relate to the duties and rights which devolved upon, and pertained to, the priests in relation to the sacrifices. Although many of the instructions are necessarily repeated from the general regulations, as to the different kinds of sacrifice and the mode of presenting them; most of them are new, and of great importance in relation to the institution of sacrifice generally. <div eID="gen1213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1214" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lev.6.1-Lev.6.7">Lev 6:1-7</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_5:14-6:7)<note placement="foot">In the original the division of verses in the Hebrew text is followed; but we have thought it better to keep to the arrangement adopted in our English version. - Tr.</note>
entries.c1f37cb163085156dbdc591c9c04087b3de1f765: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.8">Lev 6:8</reference> <div eID="gen1214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1215" type="x-p"/> (Hebrew_Bible_vv_1-6). The Law of the Burnt-Offering commences the series, and special reference is made to the daily burnt-offering (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.42">Exo 29:38-42</reference>). <div eID="gen1215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1216" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">It, the burnt-offering, shall</hi> (burn) <hi type="italic">upon the hearth upon the altar the whole night till the morning, and the fire of the altar be kept burning with it</hi>.” The verb תּוּקד is wanting in the first clause, and only introduced in the second; but it belongs to the first clause as well. The pronoun הוא at the opening of the sentence cannot stand for the verb to be in the imperative. The passages, which <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> adduces in support of this, are of a totally different kind. The instructions apply primarily to the burnt-offering, which was offered every evening, and furnished the basis for all the burnt-offerings (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.39">Exo 29:38-39</reference>; Num 33:3-4).
entries.25c08d66660b9ec423b7b9667a09ddbb498924b3: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.10-Lev.6.11">Lev 6:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen1216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1217" type="x-p"/> In the morning of every day the priest was to put on his linen dress (see <reference osisRef="Exod.28.42">Exo 28:42</reference>) and the white drawers, and lift off, i.e., clear away, the ashes to which the fire had consumed the burnt-offering upon the altar (אכל is construed with a double accusative, to consume the sacrifice to ashes), and pour them down beside the altar (see <reference osisRef="Lev.1.16">Lev 1:16</reference>). The ו in מדּו is not to be regarded as the old form of the connecting vowel, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.24">Gen 1:24</reference> (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §211 <hi type="italic">b</hi>; see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §90, 3 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), but as the suffix, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.8">2Sa 20:8</reference>, although the use of the suffix with the governing noun in the construct state can only be found in other cases in the poetical writings (cf. <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §121 <hi type="italic">b</hi>; <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, 291 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). He was then to take off his official dress, and having put on other (ordinary) clothes, to take away the ashes from the court, and carry them out of the camp to a clean place. The priest was only allowed to approach the altar in his official dress; but he could not go out of the camp with this.
entries.3e9dc89572b1c828c7175aa72c30d44ae30911d0: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.12">Lev 6:12</reference> <div eID="gen1217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1218" type="x-p"/> The fire of the altar was also to be kept burning “<hi type="italic">with it</hi>” (בּו, viz., the burnt-offering) the whole day through without going out. For this purpose the priest was to burn wood upon it (the altar-fire), and lay the burnt-offering in order upon it, and cause the fat portions of the peace-offerings to ascend in smoke, - that is to say, whenever peace-offerings were brought, for they were not prescribed for every day.
entries.b014a683d39700a82ec57d7c8662865167619589: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.13">Lev 6:13</reference> <div eID="gen1218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1219" type="x-p"/> Fire was to be kept constantly burning upon the altar without going out, not in order that the heavenly fire, which proceeded from Jehovah when Aaron and his sons first entered upon the service of the altar after their consecration, and consumed the burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, might never be extinguished (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.9.24">Lev 9:24</reference>); but that the burnt-offering might never go out, because this was the divinely appointed symbol and visible sign of the uninterrupted worship of Jehovah, which the covenant nation could never suspend either day or night, without being unfaithful to its calling. For the same reason other nations also kept perpetual fire burning upon the altars of their principal gods. (For proofs, see <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi> and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> ad h. l.)
entries.0a91bff73d940724dfc328e5b63bfaad1e165901: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.14-Lev.6.18">Lev 6:14-18</reference> <div eID="gen1219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1220" type="x-p"/> The Law of the Meat-Offering. - The regulations in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.14">Lev 6:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.15">Lev 6:15</reference>, are merely a repetition of <reference osisRef="Lev.2.2">Lev 2:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.2.3">Lev 2:3</reference>; but in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.16-Lev.6.18">Lev 6:16-18</reference> the new instructions are introduced with regard to what was left and had not been burned upon the altar. The priests were to eat this as unleavened, i.e., to bake it without leaven, and to eat it in a holy place, viz., in the court of the tabernacle. תּאכל מצות in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.16">Lev 6:16</reference> is explained by “<hi type="italic">it shall not be baken with leaven</hi>” in Lev 6:17. It was the priests’ share of the firings of Jehovah (see <reference osisRef="Lev.1.9">Lev 1:9</reference>), and as such it was most holy (see <reference osisRef="Lev.2.3">Lev 2:3</reference>), like the sin-offering and trespass-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.25">Lev 6:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.26">Lev 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.7.6">Lev 7:6</reference>), and only to be eaten by the male members of the families of the priests. This was to be maintained as a statute for ever (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.3.17">Lev 3:17</reference>). <hi type="italic">Every one that touches them</hi> (the most holy offerings) <hi type="italic">becomes holy</hi>.” יקדּשׁ does not mean he shall be holy, or shall sanctify himself (lxx, <hi type="italic">Vulg., Luth., a Lap.,</hi> etc.), nor he is consecrated to the sanctuary and is to perform service there (<hi type="italic">Theodor</hi>., <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, and others). In this provision, which was equally applicable to the sin-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.27">Lev 6:27</reference>), to the altar of the burnt-offering (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.37">Exo 29:37</reference>), and to the most holy vessels of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.29">Exo 30:29</reference>), the word is not to be interpreted by Num 17:2-3, or <reference osisRef="Deut.22.9">Deu 22:9</reference>, or by the expression “shall be holy” in <reference osisRef="Lev.27.10">Lev 27:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.21">Lev 27:21</reference>, and Num 18:10, but by <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa 65:5</reference>, “touch me not, for I am holy.” The idea is this, every layman who touched these most holy things became holy through the contact, so that henceforth he had to guard against defilement in the same manner as the sanctified priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.1-Lev.21.8">Lev 21:1-8</reference>), though without sharing the priestly rights and prerogatives. This necessarily placed him in a position which would involve many inconveniences in connection with ordinary life.
entries.4361fd93e0cface91df2e4c4bfd0a363f54cb428: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23">Lev 6:19-23</reference> <div eID="gen1220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1221" type="x-p"/> The Meat-Offering of the Priests is introduced, as a new law, with a special formula, and is inserted here in its proper place in the sacrificial instructions given for the priests, as it would have been altogether out of place among the general laws for the laity. In “<hi type="italic">the day of his anointing</hi>” (המּשׁח, construed as a passive with the accusative as in <reference osisRef="Gen.4.18">Gen 4:18</reference>), Aaron and his sons were to offer a <hi type="italic">corban</hi> as “<hi type="italic">a perpetual meat-offering</hi>” (<hi type="italic">minchah</hi>, in the absolute instead of the construct state: cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.29.42">Exo 29:42</reference>; Num 28:6; see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §116, 6, Note <hi type="italic">b</hi>); and this was to be done in all future time by “<hi type="italic">the priest who was anointed of his sons in his stead,</hi>” that is to say, by every high priest at the time of his consecration. “<hi type="italic">In the day of his anointing:</hi>” when the anointing was finished, the seven were designated as “the <hi type="italic">day</hi>,” like the seven days of creation in Gen 2:4. This <hi type="italic">minchah</hi> was not offered during the seven days of the anointing itself, but after the consecration was finished, i.e., in all probability, as the Jewish tradition assumes, at the beginning of the eighth day, when the high priest entered upon his office, viz., along with the daily morning sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.39">Exo 29:38-39</reference>), and before the offering described in Lev 9. It then continued to be offered, as “a perpetual <hi type="italic">minchah</hi>,” every morning and evening during the whole term of his office, according to the testimony of the book of Wis. Wis.(45:14, where we cannot suppose the daily burnt-offering to be intended) and also of Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> 3:10, 7).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid., Lundius, jüd. Heiligthümer,</hi> B. 3, c 9, §17 and 19; <hi type="italic">Thalhofer ut supra,</hi> p. 139; and <hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi> on the Epistle to the Hebrews. The text evidently enjoins the offering of this <hi type="italic">minchah</hi> upon Aaron alone; for though Aaron and his sons are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.13">Lev 6:13</reference>, as they were consecrated together, in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.15">Lev 6:15</reference> the priest anointed of his sons in Aaron’s stead, i.e., the successor of Aaron in the high-priesthood, is commanded to offer it. Consequently the view maintained by <hi type="italic">Maimonides</hi>, <hi type="italic">Abarbanel</hi>, and others, which did not become general even among the Rabbins, viz., that every ordinary priest was required to offer this meat-offering when entering upon his office, has no solid foundation in the law (see <hi type="italic">Selden de success. in pontif.</hi> ii. c. 9; <hi type="italic">L' Empereur ad Middoth</hi> 1, 4, Not. 8; and <hi type="italic">Thalhofer</hi>, p. 150).</note> <div eID="gen1221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1222" type="x-p"/> It was to consist of the tenth of an ephah of fine flour, one half of which was to be presented in the morning, the other in the evening; - not as flour, however, but made in a pan with oil, “<hi type="italic">roasted</hi>” and פּתּים מנחת ני תּפי (“<hi type="italic">broken pieces of a</hi> <hi type="italic">minchah</hi> <hi type="italic">of crumbs</hi>”), i.e., in broken pieces, like a <hi type="italic">minchah</hi> composed of crumbs. מרבּכת (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.14">Lev 6:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.29">1Ch 23:29</reference>) is no doubt synonymous with מרבּכת סלת, and to be understood as denoting fine flour sufficiently burned or roasted in oil; the meaning mixed or mingled does not harmonise with <reference osisRef="Lev.7.12">Lev 7:12</reference>, where the mixing or kneading with oil is expressed by בּשּׁמן בּלוּלת. The <hi type="italic">hapax legomenon</hi> תּפיני signifies either broken or baked, according as we suppose the word to be derived from the Arabic <hi type="italic">'afana</hi> diminuit, or, as Gesenius and the Rabbins do, from אפה to bake, a point which can hardly be decided with certainty. This <hi type="italic">minchah</hi>, which was also instituted as a perpetual ordinance, was to be burnt entirely upon the altar, like every meat-offering presented by a priest, because it belonged to the category of the burnt-offerings, and of these meat-offerings the offerer himself had no share (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.3">Lev 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.10">Lev 2:10</reference>). <hi type="italic">Origen</hi> observes in his <hi type="italic">homil</hi>. iv. in Levit.: <hi type="italic">In caeteris quidem praeceptis pontifex in offerendis sacrificiis populo praebet officium, in hoc vero mandato quae propria sunt curat et quod ad se spectat exequitur</hi>. It is also to be observed that the high priest was to offer only a bloodless <hi type="italic">minchah</hi> for himself, and not a bleeding sacrifice, which would have pointed to expiation. As the sanctified of the Lord, he was to draw near to the Lord every day with a sacrificial gift, which shadowed forth the fruits of sanctification.
entries.a6e8f9e11d650586104614b09aebb3a73f006ef9: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.24-Lev.6.27">Lev 6:24-27</reference> <div eID="gen1222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1223" type="x-p"/> The Law of the Sin-Offering, which is introduced with a new introductory formula on account of the interpolation of <reference osisRef="Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23">Lev 6:19-23</reference>, gives more precise instructions, though chiefly with regard to the sin-offerings of the laity, first as to the place of slaughtering, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.24">Lev 4:24</reference>, and then as to the most holy character of the flesh and blood of the sacrifices. The flesh of these sin-offerings was to be eaten by the priest who officiated at a holy place, in the fore-court (see <reference osisRef="Lev.6.16">Lev 6:16</reference>). Whoever touched it became holy (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.6.18">Lev 6:18</reference>); and if any one sprinkled any of the blood upon his clothes, whatever the blood was sprinkled upon was to be washed in a holy place, in order that the most holy blood might not be carried out of the sanctuary into common life along with the sprinkled clothes, and thereby be profaned. The words “thou shalt wash” in <reference osisRef="Lev.6.20">Lev 6:20</reference> are addressed to the priest.
entries.25769dd7169f1dbebfdc18e5e053c0957ee58dab: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.28">Lev 6:28</reference> <div eID="gen1223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1224" type="x-p"/> The flesh was equally holy. The vessel, in which it was boiled for the priests to eat, was to be broken in pieces if it were of earthenware, and scoured (מרק <hi type="italic">Pual</hi>) and overflowed with water, i.e., thoroughly rinsed out, if it were of copper, lest any of the most holy flesh should adhere to the vessel, and be desecrated by its being used in the preparation of common food, or for other earthly purposes. It was possible to prevent this desecration in the case of copper vessels by a thorough cleansing; but not so with earthen vessels, which absorb the fat, so that it cannot be removed by washing. The latter therefore were to be broken in pieces, i.e., thoroughly destroyed. On the other hand, earthen vessels that had been defiled were also ordered to be broken to pieces, though for the very opposite reason (see <reference osisRef="Lev.11.33">Lev 11:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.35">Lev 11:35</reference>).
entries.4482d0bbdbfd3fa7868f3f78f6311211784a6e27: <reference osisRef="Lev.6.29-Lev.6.30">Lev 6:29-30</reference> <div eID="gen1224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1225" type="x-p"/> The flesh of the sin-offering was to be eaten after it had been boiled, like the meat-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.16">Lev 6:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.6.18">Lev 6:18</reference>), by the males among the priests alone. But this only applied to the sin-offerings the laity (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.22-Lev.5.13">Lev 4:22-5:13</reference>). The flesh of the sin-offerings for the high priest and the whole congregation (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.1-Lev.4.21">Lev 4:1-21</reference>), the blood of which was brought into the tabernacle “to make atonement in the sanctuary,” i.e., that the expiation with the blood might be completed there, was not to be eaten, but to be burned with fire (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.12">Lev 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.21">Lev 4:21</reference>). - On the signification of this act of eating the flesh of the sin-offering, see at Lev 10:17.  <chapter eID="Lev.6"/> <div eID="gen1225" type="x-p"/>

entries.262a61f4dcc43c5978877597abe3e67c31af7c40: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.6.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.6.1" sID="gen13170" type="section"/> <div sID="gen13171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the Lord spake unto Moses.</hi> Moses now no longer treats of the means of expiating errors when the sinner is guilty through thoughtlessness; but he prescribes the mode of reconciliation, when any one shall have wilfully and designedly offended God. And this is well worthy of notice, lest those who may have been guilty of voluntary sin should doubt whether God will be propitiated towards them, provided they make application to the one sacrifice of Christ, in which consists the entire substance of the shadows of the Law. We must indeed beware lest we indulge ourselves under the cover of God’s clemency and readiness to pardon, — for the lust of the flesh provokes us to sin more than enough, without the addition of this snare, — nor is it less than a blasphemous insult to God to take occasion and license for sin, from the fact of His willingness to pardon. Let then the fear of God reign in us, which will repress our wicked desires like a rein, so that we should not wilfully fall into sin; and let His mercy rather engender the hatred and detestation of sin in our hearts, than incite us to audacity. Yet, at the same time, we must prudently take heed, lest if we imagine God to be inexorable to our voluntary sins, this excessive severity should overthrow the hope of salvation even in those who are the holiest. For even now-a-days there are some madmen who deny pardon to all who may have chanted to fall through the infirmity of the flesh, since to morose men this severity has its charms, and by this hallucination Novatus <note n="271"> <div sID="gen13172" type="x-p"/> Novatus, a Carthaginian Presbyter, who in conjunction with Novatian a Presbyter of Rome, was the founder of the Novatian sect, a.d. 251, also called Cathari, or Aristeri. They “considered the genuine Church of Christ to be a society, where virtue and innocence reigned universally, and refused any longer to acknowledge those as its members who had even once degenerated into unrighteousness.” — Waddington’s Church Hist., vol. 1 pp. 165, 166.<div eID="gen13172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13173" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">C.</hi> mentions, Inst., book 4, ch. 1, sect. 23, (Calvin Society’s Translation, vol. 3, p. 35,) the similarity of some of the opinions held by the Anabaptists of his day to those of the Novatians.<div eID="gen13173" type="x-p"/> </note> greatly troubled the Church of old. But if we all honestly examine ourselves, it will plainly appear that those rigid censors, who affect the reputation of sanctity by immoderate asperity, are the grossest hypocrites. For if they would abandon their pride, and examine into their lives, which of them would find himself free from concupiscence? and whose conscience must not often smite him?<div eID="gen13171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13174" type="x-p"/>It is then monstrous blindness to exalt men, clothed in human flesh, to such a pitch of perfection, as that their conscience should not convict them of any fault or blame. And nothing is more pestilent than this imposture of the devil, excluding from the hope of pardon those who knowingly and willingly have sinned; since there is not one even of God’s best servants, in whom the corrupt affections of the flesh do not sometimes prevail; for although they be neither adulterers, nor thieves, nor murderers, yet there is none whom the last Commandment of the Law — “Thou shalt not covet,” — does not convict of sin. And assuredly the more advance one has made in endeavors after purity, the more he feels and acknowledges that he is still very far from reaching its goal. Therefore, unless we would purposely close the gate of salvation against us, we must hold that God is placable towards all, who trust that their sin is forgiven them by the sacrifice of Christ; for God is neither changed, nor is our condition worse than that of the fathers, whereas under the Law God appointed sacrifices for the expiation even of voluntary offenses. Hence it follows, that although we are convicted of voluntary sin, yet a remedy is set before us in the Gospel for procuring pardon: else would these ancient figures be more than delusive, which had no other object than to be testimonies and mirrors of the grace which was finally manifested to us in Christ. If there ought to be a mutual agreement between the external representation of grace under the Law, and the spiritual effect which Christ brought in, it plainly appears that sins are no less forgiven to us now, than to the ancient people; and thus that believers are reminded by this symbol, that they are not to despair of reconciliation, whilst they take no pleasure in their sins; but rather that they should boldly seek for pardon in the perpetual sacrifice which constantly renders God favorable to all the godly. And surely since repentance and faith are the sure pledges of God’s favor, it cannot be but that they should be received into His grace who are endued with these two gifts. Besides, the remission of sins is an inestimable treasure, which God has deposited in His Church, to be the peculiar blessing of His children; as the Confession of Faith declares, “I believe in the Holy Catholic Church, the forgiveness of sins.” Nor would what Paul proclaims concerning the embassy entrusted to him be consistent, unless Christ’s satisfaction daily propitiated God towards believers. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.20">2 Corinthians 5:20</reference>.)<div eID="gen13174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13175" type="x-p"/>The question here is not about some trifling offense, but about the crime of unfaithfulness, doubled by the addition of perjury. It is true that perfidy, or deceit, or violence, are first mentioned, to mark the grossness of the sin; but the guilt lies chiefly in the profanation of God’s name when the injury done to man is sheltered under a false oath. At any rate, he is admitted to pardon who has both iniquitously deceived his brother and has impiously abused God’s name. Hence it appears that God spares wretched sinners although they may have contaminated themselves by faithlessness, and have aggravated the crime committed against men by sacrilege, having insulted God through their perjury. But although Moses only enumerates transgressions of the Eighth Commandment, still he teaches, according to his usual manner, by <hi type="italic">synecdoche </hi>what must be done in the case of other offenses also. If, then, anything shall have been taken away by violence, or by fraud, and perjury has been superadded, he commands not only that satisfaction should be made to the neighbor who is defrauded, but that the price of atonement should also be offered to God. And the reason for this is expressly given, because not only has a mortal man been injured, but God has also been offended, who would have men conduct themselves justly and reverently towards each other; and then the crime is carried to extremity by the violation of God’s sacred name. The sacrifice is not indeed required from a thief or robber, or from the denier of a deposit, or the appropriator of anything lost, unless they have also perjured themselves; yet the words of Moses are not without their weight: if any one, by the denial of a deposit, or by theft, or robbery, shall have “committed a trespass against the Lord;” whereby he signifies, that whenever an injury is inflicted on men, God in their person is offended, because every transgression of the Law violates and perverts His justice.<div eID="gen13175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13176" type="x-p"/>We shall elsewhere see more about the restitution to be made in case of theft or robbery, especially when a person has been found guilty. This point, however, is alone referred to directly in this passage, viz., that whoever injures or inflicts a loss upon his brother, incurs guilt and condemnation before God; but if he proceeds to such a pitch of obstinacy, as to cover his crime by falsely appealing to the sacred name of God, he is polluted by double iniquity, so that compensation of the damage is not sufficient, but he must also make atonement to God. But we must understand this of those who, having escaped from the fear of punishment, voluntarily repent. The notion of some commentators who alter the copula into the disjunctive particle, and consider perjury to be one of the various sins referred to, I reject as foreign to the meaning of Moses. Others explain it thus: “If any shall have committed robbery or theft, or shall have sworn falsely about a thing lawful in itself:” but I do not see why the words should be wrested thus; besides, their mistake is refitted by the context itself, in which restitution is coupled with the sacrifices, and this could not be applicable unless perjury were conjoined also with fraud or violence. Nor does the disjunctive particle which follows help them; for after he has commanded what was taken away by force or deceit to be restored, because all the various points could not be separately expressed, it is added, “Or all that about which he hath sworn falsely,” not as if the guilt of perjury had been contracted in any other matters, but that he might cut away all means of subterfuge, which the repetition also confirms; for, after having introduced the crime of swearing falsely, he again, as if more clearly explaining what he had said, commands the restitution of the principal, together with the fifth part. But what is it that he commands to be restored except what the deceiver had kept back under cover of his oath? Of this a clearer exposition will be found under the Eighth Commandment.<div eID="gen13176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13177" type="x-p"/>A satisfaction is therefore enjoined to be made towards men together with the offering. Nor is it without reason that God commands them to make up the loss on the day when the offering is made, lest hypocrites should promise themselves impunity after having enriched themselves by the property of another. It was indeed permitted them to restore their property to others before they propitiated God by the sacrifice; but God will not have His altar defiled, which would be the case if thieves or robbers offered victims belonging to others. He would, therefore, have the hands of those who sacrifice cleansed from pollution. And surely those who offer a victim to God out of spoils unjustly obtained, in some measure implicate Him as a participator in their crime.
